title: Pandas Cheatsheet
name: Pandas Cheatsheet
description: Canonical copy-paste cheatsheet for core Pandas syntax and production workflows.

entries.problem: See shape, types, missingness, and sample rows fast.
entries.trigger: You just loaded a dataset and need a first-pass audit.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")

print(df.head())
print(df.tail())
print(df.shape)
print(df.columns)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.info())
print(df.describe(include="all"))
print(df.isna().sum())
entries.minimal_notes: `info()` is the fastest way to check dtypes and non-null counts. `describe(include="all")` gives a broad summary for mixed-type frames.
entries.common_bug: Relying on `head()` only and missing dtype or null issues.

entries.problem: Read CSV, Excel, JSON, or Parquet with correct schema and memory efficiency.
entries.trigger: You need production-style ingestion from common file formats.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

csv_df = pd.read_csv(
    "sales.csv",
    usecols=["order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "amount"],
    dtype={"order_id": "string", "customer_id": "string", "amount": "float64"},
    parse_dates=["order_date"],
    na_values=["", "NA", "null"],
)
excel_df = pd.read_excel("sales.xlsx", sheet_name=0)
json_df = pd.read_json("sales.json", lines=True)
parquet_df = pd.read_parquet("sales.parquet")
entries.minimal_notes: Specify `dtype`, `usecols`, and `parse_dates` early to reduce downstream cleanup. Use the format-specific reader instead of converting through CSV.
entries.common_bug: Letting Pandas infer everything and ending up with object dtypes or slow reads.

entries.problem: Keep only the columns you need.
entries.trigger: You want a smaller working frame.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
subset = df[["order_id", "amount"]]
entries.minimal_notes: Column selection is the simplest way to reduce memory and focus operations.
entries.common_bug: Using a single bracket and accidentally selecting a Series.

entries.problem: Filter by membership or numeric range.
entries.trigger: You need set-based or interval-based selection.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"score": [10, 35, 70], "status": ["new", "paid", "open"]})
filtered = df[df["status"].isin(["paid", "open"]) & df["score"].between(20, 80)]
entries.minimal_notes: `isin` and `between` are vectorized and easy to read.
entries.common_bug: Using chained comparisons incorrectly with Series objects.

entries.problem: Order records deterministically.
entries.trigger: You need reproducible outputs or top-ranked rows.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [2, 1, 1], "score": [10, 30, 20]})
sorted_df = df.sort_values(["customer_id", "score"], ascending=[True, False])
sorted_idx = sorted_df.set_index("customer_id").sort_index()
entries.minimal_notes: Sort before deduplication when recency or priority matters.
entries.common_bug: Sorting by strings when you expected numeric or datetime order.

entries.problem: Manage frame schema explicitly.
entries.trigger: You need controlled column lifecycle operations.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
df = df.rename(columns={"a": "x"})
df.insert(1, "y", [10, 20])
removed = df.pop("b")
df = df.drop(columns=["x"])
entries.minimal_notes: Use `insert` for stable column placement and `pop` when you want the removed data.
entries.common_bug: Mutating temporary slices and assuming the parent frame changed.

entries.problem: Create derived features or update existing values safely.
entries.trigger: You need copy-safe transformations.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"amount": [100, 200, 300]})
df = df.assign(amount_usd=lambda x: x["amount"] * 1.08)

patch = pd.DataFrame({"amount": [^999]}, index=[^1])
df.update(patch)
entries.minimal_notes: `assign` is chain-friendly. `update` writes aligned non-null values into matching labels.
entries.common_bug: Expecting `update` to add new rows or columns.

entries.problem: Detect, drop, fill, interpolate, and combine sparse data.
entries.trigger: Your data has gaps.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [None, 2, 3]})
df["a"] = df["a"].fillna(0)
df["b"] = df["b"].ffill()
clean = df.dropna(subset=["a"])
combined = df["a"].combine_first(df["b"])
entries.minimal_notes: `fillna`, `ffill`, `bfill`, `dropna`, and `combine_first` cover most missing-data workflows.
entries.common_bug: Filling numeric data with strings and silently changing dtype to object.

entries.problem: Deduplicate records and keep the right row.
entries.trigger: You suspect repeated rows or keys.
entries.minimal_notes: Sort before `drop_duplicates` when recency matters.
entries.common_bug: Dropping full-row duplicates when duplicate keys matter more than exact row equality.

entries.problem: Normalize columns to modern nullable dtypes.
entries.trigger: You need consistent missing-value semantics.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv").convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="numpy_nullable")
df["amount"] = df["amount"].astype("Float64")
df["flag"] = df["flag"].astype("boolean")
entries.minimal_notes: Prefer nullable dtypes over legacy object columns. Use Arrow-backed dtypes when your pipeline benefits from them.
entries.common_bug: Leaving numeric data as object dtype and slowing all downstream operations.

entries.problem: Convert text to timestamps or durations.
entries.trigger: You need time-series operations.
entries.minimal_notes: `errors="coerce"` is useful for dirty input. Parse time values before arithmetic.
entries.common_bug: Comparing naive and timezone-aware timestamps.

entries.problem: Attach or convert timezones correctly.
entries.trigger: You work with timestamps across regions.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"ts": pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=3, freq="D")})
df["ts_utc"] = df["ts"].dt.tz_localize("UTC")
df["ts_oslo"] = df["ts_utc"].dt.tz_convert("Europe/Oslo")
entries.minimal_notes: `tz_localize` attaches a timezone; `tz_convert` changes it.
entries.common_bug: Calling `tz_convert` on naive timestamps.

entries.problem: Clean and parse text columns.
entries.trigger: You need normalization or token extraction.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"email": [" Alice@Example.com ", "bob@test.org"]})
df["email_clean"] = df["email"].str.strip().str.lower()
df["domain"] = df["email_clean"].str.extract(r"@(.+)$")
df["first_token"] = df["email_clean"].str.split("@").str[^0]
entries.minimal_notes: Chain `.str` methods for vectorized string operations. `extractall` is useful when you expect multiple regex matches.
entries.common_bug: Applying Python string methods directly to a Series.

entries.problem: Control category sets, ordering, and codes.
entries.trigger: You need predictable label behavior and smaller memory use.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["low", "high", "low"], categories=["low", "medium", "high"], ordered=True))
s = s.cat.set_categories(["low", "medium", "high", "critical"], ordered=True)
s = s.cat.remove_unused_categories()
codes = s.cat.codes
entries.minimal_notes: Use ordered categories for explicit sort semantics. Remove unused categories after filtering.
entries.common_bug: Sorting or comparing unordered categories and getting unexpected results.

entries.problem: Join two tables on keys with cardinality checks.
entries.trigger: You need relational enrichment.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "amount": [10, 20]})
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "country": ["NO", "SE"]})

merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="one_to_one")
entries.minimal_notes: Use `validate` to catch key cardinality errors early.
entries.common_bug: Merge explosions from duplicate keys on either side.

entries.problem: Stack batches or compare related tables.
entries.trigger: You need batch assembly or difference detection.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "value": [10, 20]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [3, 4], "value": [30, 40]})

combined = pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)
diff = a.compare(a.copy())
entries.minimal_notes: Use `concat` for batch append patterns, not repeated concatenation in loops. `compare` helps debug differences.
entries.common_bug: Assuming `concat` performs a keyed join.

entries.problem: Summarize data by one or more keys.
entries.trigger: You need totals, counts, or custom summaries.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["NO", "NO", "SE"], "amount": [10, 15, 20]})
summary = (
    df.groupby("region", as_index=False, observed=True, dropna=False)
    .agg(total_amount=("amount", "sum"), avg_amount=("amount", "mean"))
)
entries.minimal_notes: Named aggregations keep output columns readable. `observed=True` helps with categorical group keys.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting `as_index=False` and getting grouped keys in the index.

entries.problem: Add group-level metrics back to each row.
entries.trigger: You need per-row features like group mean or share.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["NO", "NO", "SE"], "amount": [10, 15, 20]})
g = df.groupby("region")
df["region_avg"] = g["amount"].transform("mean")
df["region_cumcount"] = g.cumcount()
df["region_total_rank"] = g["amount"].rank(method="dense", ascending=False)
entries.minimal_notes: `transform` preserves row count and aligns back to the original frame. `cumcount` and grouped `rank` are common feature-engineering tools.
entries.common_bug: Using `agg` when you actually need same-length output.

entries.problem: Convert long data to wide layout with and without aggregation.
entries.trigger: You need matrix-style output or aggregated reshaping.
entries.minimal_notes: Use `pivot` for unique combinations and `pivot_table` for duplicate cells.
entries.common_bug: Using `pivot` when duplicates require aggregation.

entries.problem: Normalize wide data into tidy rows.
entries.trigger: You need a long format for analysis or plotting.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "sales_q1": [10, 20], "sales_q2": [15, 25]})
long = df.melt(id_vars=["id"], var_name="quarter", value_name="sales")
entries.minimal_notes: `melt` is the standard inverse of wide-to-long reshaping. `wide_to_long` is useful for systematic column prefixes.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to preserve identifier columns in `id_vars`.

entries.problem: Move index levels between rows and columns.
entries.trigger: You are working with hierarchical indexes.
entries.minimal_notes: `stack` and `unstack` are common in multi-indexed workflows.
entries.common_bug: Mixing index level names and positions incorrectly.

entries.problem: Compute moving statistics.
entries.trigger: You need trailing window features.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
rolling_mean = s.rolling(window=3, min_periods=1).mean()
entries.minimal_notes: `rolling` is the usual choice for moving averages and volatility.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting `min_periods` and getting leading NaNs.

entries.problem: Compute cumulative and exponentially weighted statistics.
entries.trigger: You need growing-history or smoothed features.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
exp_mean = s.expanding(min_periods=1).mean()
ewm_mean = s.ewm(alpha=0.3, adjust=False).mean()
entries.minimal_notes: `expanding` uses all prior rows; `ewm` is common for trend tracking and online metrics.
entries.common_bug: Using `rolling` when you actually need full-history accumulation.

entries.problem: Change time frequency and aggregate.
entries.trigger: Your index is datetime-like.
entries.minimal_notes: `resample` is the time-series equivalent of groupby by time bins.
entries.common_bug: Resampling a non-datetime index.

entries.problem: Fill gaps in ordered numeric data.
entries.trigger: You have sparse series with intermediate gaps.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1.0, None, None, 4.0])
filled = s.interpolate(method="linear")
entries.minimal_notes: Interpolation is best for continuous ordered data, especially time series.
entries.common_bug: Using interpolation on unordered categorical data.

entries.problem: Extract date parts or normalize timestamps.
entries.trigger: You need year, month, weekday, or timezone-aware operations.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"ts": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-07-06"], utc=True)})
df["year"] = df["ts"].dt.year
df["month"] = df["ts"].dt.month
df["weekday"] = df["ts"].dt.weekday
df["date_only"] = df["ts"].dt.normalize()
entries.minimal_notes: `.dt` is the vectorized datetime accessor. Use `floor`, `ceil`, and `round` for time bucketing.
entries.common_bug: Calling `.dt` on object dtype values that are not parsed datetimes.

entries.problem: Make fast exploratory plots.
entries.trigger: You need a visual sanity check.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [10, 15, 13, 18], "group": ["a", "a", "b", "b"]})
ax1 = df.plot(x="x", y="y", kind="line", title="Line")
ax2 = df["y"].plot(kind="hist", bins=4, title="Hist")
ax3 = df.plot(x="x", y="y", kind="scatter", title="Scatter")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `.plot` is good for fast diagnostics and simple summaries. Keep visual checks lightweight.
entries.common_bug: Expecting publication-quality control from the default plot accessor.

entries.problem: Find large columns or reduce memory usage.
entries.trigger: You need to scale a frame without wasting RAM.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(df.memory_usage(deep=True))
print(df.info(memory_usage="deep"))
df["status"] = df["status"].astype("category")
df = df.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="numpy_nullable")
entries.minimal_notes: `deep=True` matters for object columns. Categoricals and nullable dtypes often reduce memory materially.
entries.common_bug: Underestimating memory because object/string storage is not counted deeply.

entries.problem: Write a result table to CSV safely.
entries.trigger: You need a shareable flat-file output.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "value": [10, 20]})
df.to_csv("output.csv", index=False)
entries.minimal_notes: `index=False` is usually the right default for exchange files.
entries.common_bug: Accidentally exporting the index as an extra column.

entries.problem: Save columnar analytics data.
entries.trigger: You need compact, fast IO.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "value": [10, 20]})
df.to_parquet("output.parquet", index=False)
entries.minimal_notes: Parquet is usually better than CSV for large analytics pipelines.
entries.common_bug: Ignoring dtype preservation and schema consistency.

entries.problem: Flatten nested JSON records.
entries.trigger: Your input has nested dict/list structures.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

records = [
    {"id": 1, "user": {"name": "Alice", "country": "NO"}},
    {"id": 2, "user": {"name": "Bob", "country": "SE"}},
]
df = pd.json_normalize(records)
entries.minimal_notes: `json_normalize` is the standard way to flatten nested mappings.
entries.common_bug: Attempting manual nested extraction for large payloads.

entries.problem: Build null masks.
entries.trigger: You need to filter or count missing data.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, None, 3])
mask = pd.isna(s)
not_missing = pd.notna(s)
entries.minimal_notes: Use `isna` / `notna` instead of comparing to `None`.
entries.common_bug: Comparing directly with `== None` or `!= None`.

entries.problem: Recover from object dtypes and dirty null-heavy inputs.
entries.trigger: You inherited messy columns or mixed types.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": ["1", "2", None, "4"], "y": [1, None, 3, 4]})
df = df.infer_objects(copy=False)
df = df.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="numpy_nullable")
df["x"] = pd.to_numeric(df["x"], errors="coerce")
entries.minimal_notes: `convert_dtypes()` is the preferred modern first step. `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` is useful when Arrow-backed dtypes are desired and supported.
entries.common_bug: Leaving messy data as object dtype and pushing the problem downstream.

entries.problem: Combine objects by label, not position.
entries.trigger: You need aligned arithmetic or paired transforms.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.Series([1, 2], index=["x", "y"])
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=["y", "z"])

left, right = a.align(b, join="outer")
sum_series = left.fillna(0) + right.fillna(0)
entries.minimal_notes: Alignment is label-based, not positional.
entries.common_bug: Assuming two objects line up by row order.

entries.problem: Load from or export to a database table.
entries.trigger: Your source of truth is a relational database.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///example.db")

df = pd.read_sql("SELECT order_id, amount FROM sales", engine)
df.to_sql("sales_export", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)
entries.minimal_notes: `read_sql` and `to_sql` are the standard round-trip APIs for database workflows. Prefer explicit column selection and controlled writes.
entries.common_bug: Writing the DataFrame index as an unintended database column.

entries.problem: Check representative records, value distribution, and row counts.
entries.trigger: You need a quick data sanity check.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")

sample = df.sample(n=5, random_state=42)
print(df["status"].value_counts(dropna=False))
print(df["customer_id"].nunique(dropna=True))
print(df["status"].mode())
entries.minimal_notes: `sample` is useful for spot-checking records. `value_counts()` and `nunique()` are fast for distribution checks.
entries.common_bug: Sampling without `random_state` and getting non-reproducible results.

entries.problem: Use label-based or position-based indexing precisely.
entries.trigger: You need row/column slices or scalar access.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [10, 20, 30], "b": [100, 200, 300]}, index=["x", "y", "z"])

label_slice = df.loc["x":"y", ["a", "b"]]
pos_slice = df.iloc[0:2, 0:1]
scalar_label = df.at["y", "a"]
scalar_pos = df.iat[1, 0]
entries.minimal_notes: `loc` is label-based and inclusive on slices; `iloc` is position-based. Use `at` and `iat` for scalar reads/writes.
entries.common_bug: Mixing label and position semantics or assuming `iloc` accepts labels.

entries.problem: Filter with readable boolean expressions.
entries.trigger: You want SQL-like row filtering.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"amount": [50, 200, 150], "status": ["paid", "paid", "open"]})
high_value = df.query("amount > 100 and status == 'paid'")
entries.minimal_notes: `query` keeps chained filters easier to read. It is especially useful for compact business rules.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that `query` still obeys Python operator precedence inside expressions.

entries.problem: Select rows by clock time or first/last valid timestamps.
entries.trigger: You work with intraday or sparse time series.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.date_range("2026-07-01", periods=6, freq="6H")
df = pd.DataFrame({"value": range(6)}, index=idx)

business_hours = df.between_time("09:00", "17:00")
first_ts = df.first_valid_index()
last_ts = df.last_valid_index()
entries.minimal_notes: `between_time` works on a DatetimeIndex. `first_valid_index` and `last_valid_index` help with sparse series.
entries.common_bug: Calling time-based index methods on a non-datetime index.

entries.problem: Rank values or extract top records per group.
entries.trigger: You need leaderboard-style outputs.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["a", "a", "b"], "score": [10, 30, 20]})
df["rank"] = df["score"].rank(method="dense", ascending=False)
top2 = df.nlargest(2, "score")
bottom2 = df.nsmallest(2, "score")
entries.minimal_notes: `nlargest` and `nsmallest` are faster than full sorts for small top-N selections.
entries.common_bug: Using `sort_values().head()` when only top-N is needed on large data.

entries.problem: Transform scalar values, map labels, or run row/column functions.
entries.trigger: You need targeted value replacement or a function-based transform.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"status": ["new", "open", "paid"], "amount": [10, 20, 30]})
df["status"] = df["status"].replace({"new": "fresh"})
df["status_code"] = df["status"].map({"fresh": 1, "open": 2, "paid": 3})
df["amount_plus_1"] = df["amount"].apply(lambda x: x + 1)
entries.minimal_notes: Prefer vectorized operations first. Use `map` for one-to-one label lookup and `apply` only when needed.
entries.common_bug: Using `apply` for simple arithmetic that should be vectorized.

entries.problem: Apply a scalar-to-scalar function across a DataFrame.
entries.trigger: You need elementwise transformation, not row logic.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
squared = df.map(lambda x: x * x)
entries.minimal_notes: `DataFrame.map` is the current elementwise API. Use it instead of old `applymap` patterns.
entries.common_bug: Using elementwise mapping when a vectorized column operation is much faster.

entries.problem: Keep transformations readable and composable.
entries.trigger: You want pipeline-style code without temporary variables.
entries.minimal_notes: `pipe` helps when a transformation is reusable or conditional.
entries.common_bug: Inlining long transformation chains without clear step boundaries.

entries.problem: Detect changes between datasets or test outputs.
entries.trigger: You need regression checks or debug diffs.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd
from pandas.testing import assert_frame_equal

left = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 5]})

diff = left.compare(right, keep_shape=True, keep_equal=False)
assert_frame_equal(left, left.copy())
entries.minimal_notes: `compare` is useful for debugging row/column deltas. `assert_frame_equal` is the standard testing utility.
entries.common_bug: Assuming visually similar frames are equal without checking dtypes or index labels.

entries.problem: Generate aligned time indexes and business calendars.
entries.trigger: You need scheduled periods or trading-day-like sequences.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

days = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=5, freq="D")
biz = pd.bdate_range("2026-01-01", periods=5)
next_month = days + pd.offsets.MonthBegin(1)
entries.minimal_notes: Use frequency-aware constructors for repeatable time indexes. Offsets make calendar arithmetic explicit.
entries.common_bug: Hand-rolling date increments and missing weekends or month-boundary behavior.

entries.problem: Move keys into the index or restore them back to columns.
entries.trigger: You need alignment, hierarchical indexing, or time-series indexing.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "amount": [10, 20]})
indexed = df.set_index("customer_id")
restored = indexed.reset_index()
entries.minimal_notes: Explicit index strategy helps joins, resampling, and alignment.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting which key is stored in the index and which is a column.

entries.problem: Work with hierarchical row or column labels.
entries.trigger: You need grouped axes or nested keys.
entries.minimal_notes: `xs`, `swaplevel`, `reorder_levels`, and `droplevel` are the main MultiIndex tools.
entries.common_bug: Sorting or slicing a MultiIndex without knowing the active level order.

entries.problem: Keep complex filters and computed expressions readable.
entries.trigger: You want compact, chain-friendly logic.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [10, 20, 30]})
filtered = df.query("a > 1 and b < 30")
df["c"] = df.eval("a + b")
entries.minimal_notes: `query` and `eval` can make pipeline code easier to scan.
entries.common_bug: Expecting `eval` to replace proper schema or validation checks.

entries.problem: Join ordered time series by nearest key or ordered key.
entries.trigger: You need as-of or ordered alignment.
entries.minimal_notes: Both frames must be sorted for `merge_asof`. `merge_ordered` is useful for ordered data with optional filling.
entries.common_bug: Calling `merge_asof` on unsorted keys.

entries.problem: Keep or pick rows from specific groups.
entries.trigger: You need first/last/nth or conditional group filtering.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["NO", "NO", "SE"], "amount": [10, 15, 20]})
g = df.groupby("region")
top_row = g.nth(0)
first_rows = g.first()
large_groups = g.filter(lambda x: len(x) >= 2)
entries.minimal_notes: `first`, `last`, `nth`, `size`, and `filter` cover most group-level row selection tasks.
entries.common_bug: Using `apply` for simple row picking logic.

entries.problem: Turn list values into one row per element.
entries.trigger: You have nested list data in a column.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "tags": [["a", "b"], ["c"]]})
exploded = df.explode("tags", ignore_index=True)
entries.minimal_notes: `explode` is common after JSON parsing or tokenization.
entries.common_bug: Exploding columns that still contain mixed scalar and list values.

entries.problem: Compute rolling windows within groups.
entries.trigger: You need per-entity time-series features.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "customer_id": [1, 1, 1, 2, 2],
        "ts": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-01", "2026-01-02"]),
        "amount": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50],
    }
).sort_values(["customer_id", "ts"])

df["rolling_2"] = (
    df.groupby("customer_id")["amount"]
      .rolling(2, min_periods=1)
      .mean()
      .reset_index(level=0, drop=True)
)
entries.minimal_notes: Sort before grouped rolling. Reset the grouped index after the rolling operation.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to sort within each group before applying a rolling window.

entries.problem: Reindex time series to a fixed frequency.
entries.trigger: You need a regular grid without aggregation.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04"]))
regular = s.asfreq("D")
entries.minimal_notes: `asfreq` is for frequency conversion and alignment, not aggregation.
entries.common_bug: Using `resample` when you only need a structural frequency change.

entries.problem: Build lagged or lead features.
entries.trigger: You need previous or future values.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"value": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
df["lag_1"] = df["value"].shift(1)
df["lead_1"] = df["value"].shift(-1)
df["pct_change"] = df["value"].pct_change()
entries.minimal_notes: `shift` is the core lag/lead primitive. `pct_change` is a common derived metric.
entries.common_bug: Mixing shifted data with unshifted labels and leaking future information.

entries.problem: Compute descriptive stats, correlation, covariance, and quantiles.
entries.trigger: You need quick statistical profiling.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [2, 4, 6, 8]})
print(df.describe())
print(df.corr(numeric_only=True))
print(df.cov(numeric_only=True))
print(df.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75], numeric_only=True))
entries.minimal_notes: `describe`, `corr`, `cov`, and `quantile` cover most exploratory stats.
entries.common_bug: Expecting correlation on non-numeric columns without cleaning dtypes first.

entries.problem: Build running totals and running extrema.
entries.trigger: You need cumulative features.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([3, 1, 4, 2])
cum = pd.DataFrame({"s": s}).assign(
    cumsum=s.cumsum(),
    cummin=s.cummin(),
    cummax=s.cummax(),
    cumprod=s.cumprod(),
)
entries.minimal_notes: Cumulative APIs are useful for trend and threshold features.
entries.common_bug: Applying cumulative logic to unsorted data and getting misleading results.

entries.problem: Inspect frequency, uniqueness, and duplicate records.
entries.trigger: You need cardinality or quality checks.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"status": ["new", "new", "paid", "open"]})
counts = df["status"].value_counts(dropna=False)
dupe_rows = df.duplicated(keep=False)
dupe_values = df["status"].duplicated(keep=False)
entries.minimal_notes: `duplicated` is the standard duplicate detector for rows or columns.
entries.common_bug: Confusing value duplication with whole-row duplication.

entries.problem: Split structured strings and normalize text variants.
entries.trigger: You need stable text processing across encodings and separators.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd
import unicodedata

df = pd.DataFrame({"path": ["a/b/c", "x/y/z"], "text": ["café", "naïve"]})
parts = df["path"].str.partition("/")
df["text_norm"] = df["text"].map(lambda x: unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", x))
entries.minimal_notes: `partition` is useful when only the first delimiter matters. Unicode normalization helps stabilize text keys.
entries.common_bug: Treating visually identical Unicode strings as equal without normalization.

entries.problem: One-hot encode categorical columns.
entries.trigger: You need model-ready indicator columns.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Oslo", "Bergen", "Oslo"]})
encoded = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["city"], dtype="int64")
decoded = pd.from_dummies(encoded.filter(like="city_"))
entries.minimal_notes: `get_dummies` is the standard encoder; `from_dummies` helps reverse the transformation in simple cases.
entries.common_bug: One-hot encoding without controlling dtype or category drift between train and inference.

entries.problem: Create, sort, slice, and align indexes directly.
entries.trigger: You need index-level manipulation without changing data columns.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.Index(["b", "a", "c"])
sorted_idx = idx.sort_values()

df = pd.DataFrame({"value": [10, 20, 30]}, index=idx)
aligned = df.reindex(sorted_idx)
entries.minimal_notes: Index objects are immutable and central to alignment semantics.
entries.common_bug: Treating the index as if it were a normal mutable column.

entries.problem: Work with MultiIndex rows or columns cleanly.
entries.trigger: You need targeted extraction from hierarchical axes.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("NO", 2025), ("NO", 2026), ("SE", 2026)], names=["region", "year"])
df = pd.DataFrame({"value": [1, 2, 3]}, index=idx)

no = df.xs("NO", level="region")
slc = df.loc[pd.IndexSlice["NO", :], :]
entries.minimal_notes: `xs` is a concise cross-section tool. `IndexSlice` makes MultiIndex selection readable.
entries.common_bug: Mixing tuple indexing with level names without confirming the index structure.

entries.problem: Reorder hierarchical axes or remove a level.
entries.trigger: You need cleaner MultiIndex outputs.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["NO", "SE"], [2025, 2026]], names=["region", "year"])
df = pd.DataFrame({"value": [1, 2, 3, 4]}, index=idx)

df = df.sort_index()
df = df.swaplevel("region", "year").sort_index()
df = df.droplevel("region")
entries.minimal_notes: `sort_index`, `swaplevel`, and `droplevel` are core MultiIndex maintenance tools.
entries.common_bug: Operating on a MultiIndex without sorting it first.

entries.problem: Apply conditional value rules.
entries.trigger: You need bounded values or conditional replacement.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([5, 15, 25, 35])
bounded = s.clip(lower=10, upper=30)
inside = s.where(s.between(10, 30), other=pd.NA)
outside = s.mask(s.between(10, 30), other=0)
entries.minimal_notes: `where` keeps values where the condition is true; `mask` does the inverse.
entries.common_bug: Swapping `where` and `mask` logic.

entries.problem: Compute rounding, differences, and percentage changes.
entries.trigger: You need feature engineering on numeric sequences.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.123, 11.456, 12.789])
out = pd.DataFrame({
    "round_1": s.round(1),
    "diff_1": s.diff(),
    "pct_change_1": s.pct_change(),
})
entries.minimal_notes: These are fast vectorized transforms for numeric pipelines.
entries.common_bug: Using Python loops for operations Pandas already vectorizes.

entries.problem: Move data between tools or persist Python-native structures.
entries.trigger: You need quick local transfer or fast round-trips.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
df.to_clipboard(index=False)
df.to_pickle("frame.pkl")
df.to_feather("frame.feather")
df.to_orc("frame.orc")
entries.minimal_notes: Use clipboard for ad hoc transfers, pickle for Python-only round trips, and Feather/ORC for fast columnar IO.
entries.common_bug: Treating pickle as a cross-language format or secure interchange format.

entries.problem: Extract or publish tabular web data.
entries.trigger: Your data source or sink is HTML or XML.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

tables = pd.read_html("https://example.com/table.html")
df = tables[^0]

xml_df = pd.read_xml("data.xml", xpath=".//row")
entries.minimal_notes: `read_html` and `read_xml` are useful for structured web tables.
entries.common_bug: Assuming every page table has a stable schema.

entries.problem: Read large files in bounded memory.
entries.trigger: Your input is too large for a single in-memory read.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

chunks = pd.read_csv("large.csv", chunksize=100_000, usecols=["id", "amount"])
total = 0
for chunk in chunks:
    total += chunk["amount"].sum()
entries.minimal_notes: Chunked reading is the standard fallback for large CSV inputs. Combine with `usecols` and `dtype` when possible.
entries.common_bug: Loading a huge file all at once and relying on swap or memory pressure.

entries.problem: Build a deterministic transformation pipeline.
entries.trigger: You want readable, testable data preparation steps.
entries.minimal_notes: Method chaining reduces temporary state and makes pipelines easier to review.
entries.common_bug: Mixing chained transformations with hidden in-place mutations.

entries.problem: Validate outputs during development and tests.
entries.trigger: You need fast correctness checks.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd
from pandas.testing import assert_frame_equal, assert_series_equal

left = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})

assert left.equals(right)
assert_frame_equal(left, right)
assert_series_equal(left["a"], right["a"])
entries.minimal_notes: `equals` is a quick boolean check; testing utilities give stricter diffs.
entries.common_bug: Checking values only and missing dtype or index mismatches.

entries.problem: Find duplicate keys or misaligned index behavior.
entries.trigger: A join, assignment, or reshape produced unexpected results.
entries.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2], "value": [10, 20, 30]})
print(df.duplicated(subset=["id"], keep=False))
print(df.index.duplicated(keep=False))
print(df.compare(df.copy(), keep_shape=True))
entries.minimal_notes: Diagnose duplicates before merge, pivot, or dedup steps.
entries.common_bug: Assuming silent index alignment will behave like row order.

performance_checklist.recommendations: Convert repeated text columns to `category` when cardinality is low.
Use nullable or Arrow-backed dtypes for cleaner missing-data handling.
Use `memory_usage(deep=True)` and `info(memory_usage="deep")` to find expensive columns.
Prefer vectorized `.str`, `.dt`, arithmetic, `groupby`, and `transform` over Python loops.
Avoid `iterrows`; prefer vectorized code or `itertuples` for row-wise iteration.
Prefer `apply` only when no vectorized alternative exists.
Prefer `concat` for batch append patterns and avoid repeated concatenation in loops.
Prefer Parquet or Feather for large analytical outputs.
Prefer deterministic sort order before deduplication or top-N selection.
Be copy-on-write aware and avoid unnecessary intermediate copies.

production_checklist: Lock schema early with explicit dtypes.
Avoid chained assignment; assign back to the frame.
Check nulls and duplicates before modeling or export.
Prefer deterministic sort order before deduplication.
Use copy-safe transformations and clear column names.
Validate output equality and schema in tests.
Review memory usage before scaling pipelines.
Confirm export formats preserve required dtypes and missing values.
Keep method chains readable and deterministic.
Avoid hidden reliance on row order when labels matter.
